oral-bioavailability outcome.

votes, and do not treat the L1/L2 name itself as a positive or negative label.

parent-condition context may apply to the query. It is not a positive-class
probability, an experimental result, or a substitute for reasoning about the
visible structure, endpoint, assay, species, formulation, exposure, and
condition. Infer direction from the record cards first, then judge transfer from
all visible context. Do not invent a numeric similarity judgment or assume that
a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

Use general medicinal-chemistry knowledge to interpret structures, but ground
every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
hidden chain-of-thought.

claims.claim: Measured absolute oral bioavailability in humans for structurally related amide/heteroaromatic drugs is predominantly above 20%: imidafenacin 57.8%, tolvaptan 56%, ACT-1004-1239 53%, lenvatinib in the order of 85%, and bromazepam 86%.
The closest benzamide-indazole analog venadaparib showed good oral bioavailability in patients and 70.63% F in mice.

L4 records show that lipophilic N-methyl amide/heteroaromatic compounds can be well absorbed despite low aqueous solubility: piroxicam has human fa ~100% and negligible first-pass metabolism with aqueous solubility ~14 µg/mL; sorafenib shows high Caco-2 permeability with P-gp efflux; vismodegib is BCS class II with high permeability.

L5 gut-wall efflux records for structurally related amide/indazole/heteroaromatic compounds show high absorptive permeability and low or non-limiting efflux: an N-methyl benzamide analog had high Caco-2 permeability with absorption not limiting; indazole amides showed high flux or modest permeability with efflux ratio near 1; amide/heteroaromatic compounds showed high permeability with efflux ratio below 2 and no significant P-gp involvement.

Even for the P-gp substrate sorafenib, oral administration to Abcb1a/1b-/- and Abcg2-/- mice showed no difference in systemic exposure versus wild type, indicating intestinal ABCB1 and ABCG2 do not play a major role in its oral bioavailability; sorafenib was also classified as highly permeable.

Low-solubility records for regorafenib, tranilast, nitazoxanide, and other lipophilic compounds do not provide an affirmative threshold-relevant low-F outcome for the query; low solubility alone does not establish F < 20%.
A few L5 records show moderate permeability or efflux ratios, but none provide an affirmative threshold-relevant low-F outcome for the query.
